name: Cape Cod Colonial

revival_periods.note: Royal Barry Wills, who founded his Boston practice in 1925, made the Cape the single most-built American house form of the post-war years; the FHA minimum house of 1946–55 is essentially a Cape.

geography.hearth: Cape Cod and the outer Massachusetts coast, where the wind is the governing design load

lineage.note: The one-and-a-half-storey cottage with a low plate and a loft in the roof is the English yeoman cottage, simplified and stiffened against the North Atlantic.

description.short: A one-and-a-half-storey, low-eaved, central-chimney cottage built to present as little surface as possible to the wind, and grown one bay at a time as a family could afford it.
description.long:
The Cape is the most economical house New England ever produced, and every one of its features is a consequence of that. There is no second storey, so there is no second plate, no second floor frame and no stair worth the name — just a steep winder beside the chimney to a loft under the rafters. The eave sits eight to nine and a half feet above the floor, which puts the head of the first-floor window within a foot of the cornice and leaves nothing for a frieze. The roof runs forty to forty-five degrees, steep enough to shed snow and to make the loft habitable, shallow enough that it does not act as a sail. And the whole building hunkers: no raised basement, no water table of consequence, no projections, no overhangs beyond a four-to-six-inch rake. On the outer Cape, where the sand offers nothing to anchor to and the wind comes off open water, a house shaped like this is a house that is still there in a hundred years.

What makes the Cape genuinely interesting as a kit of parts is that it is a growth grammar rather than a single form, and the grammar is legible on the facade. A quarter Cape has a door and one window. A half Cape has a door at one end and two windows beside it. A three-quarter Cape adds a single window on the other side of the door. A full Cape has two windows each side of a centred door. Families built the half and added to it as money and children arrived, moving the door or reframing it toward the centre. The chimney stays put through all of this, which means that in a half or three-quarter Cape the chimney is not centred on the facade — and that off-centre stack is the honest signature of an unfinished growth sequence, not a mistake.

The name is not local. Timothy Dwight, president of Yale, coined 'Cape Cod house' after travelling the peninsula in 1800; the description was published posthumously in his Travels in New England and New York (1821–22). The people who built them called them houses.

Inside, the Cape is small, warm and unexpectedly good. Two rooms flank the stack on the ground floor with the entry porch between; ceilings run seven feet; the loft above is reached by the winder and lit by gable windows only. The rooms are square, the fireplaces are close, and everything is within a few steps of everything else. There is a reason the twentieth century could not leave it alone: the plan is close to irreducible, and a family of four fits into eight hundred square feet of it without friction.

defining_characteristics: One to one-and-a-half storeys with no full second floor; the upper rooms are within the roof volume
Eave 8 ft 0 in – 9 ft 6 in above finished floor, with the first-floor window head within 14 in of the cornice and no frieze
Central chimney on the ridge (full Cape) or off-centre where the house is a half or three-quarter Cape
Side-gable roof, 40–45 degrees, of wood shingle, with a shallow rake and no soffit overhang beyond about 6 in
Facade organized by the quarter / half / three-quarter / full growth grammar, with the door offset until the plan is complete
Wall of clapboard or, on the outer Cape, unpainted white-cedar shingle laid at 5–6 in exposure
No dormers, no porch, no projections; the gable ends are blind or carry one small window each
diagnostic_tells: Window heads almost touching the cornice — the single most reliable Cape tell, and the one the revival always gets wrong
A door that is not centred, with a chimney that is not centred either but in a different place
The entire house reads as roof: the wall is roughly one-third of the elevation height, the roof two-thirds
Rake trim of 4–6 in with a plain 6–12 in return at the corner, not a full modillion cornice return
No basement showing above grade; the sill sits within 18 in of the ground

distinguished_from.difference: The revival raises the eave to clear a full-height second-floor knee wall, adds a row of gabled or shed dormers on the front slope, uses an 8:12 to 10:12 pitch, gives the house a centred door with sidelights and a symmetrical five-bay front regardless of the plan behind it, and attaches a garage. Original Capes have no front dormers. If there are dormers on the street elevation, it is a twentieth-century house.
The saltbox is two full storeys at the front with an asymmetric roof; the Cape is one-and-a-half storeys with a symmetrical one. A Cape can have a rear lean-to and remain a Cape.
The 1935–50 minimal-traditional house shares the low eave and small footprint but has a shallower roof (4:12–6:12), no central chimney, a side or end chimney if any, and picture or paired windows.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The chimney stack plus two flanking rooms of a single frame bay each, with the roof sized to make the loft usable at the ridge.
typical_ratios: Full Cape 32–38 ft wide × 26–30 ft deep; half Cape 20–24 ft wide
Eave 8 ft 0 in – 9 ft 6 in; ridge 18–22 ft above grade
Wall:roof height ratio on the front elevation about 1:2
Ground-floor ceiling 6 ft 10 in – 7 ft 6 in; loft 6 ft 0 in – 7 ft 0 in at the ridge
Window opening 2 ft 8 in – 3 ft 2 in × 4 ft 4 in – 5 ft 0 in
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: One, two, three or four windows plus a door, in the growth sequence quarter–half–three-quarter–full. The rhythm is a record of household economics, not a composition.

massing_affinities.note: The full Cape plan: two rooms flanking the stack.
The half Cape, one room and a stack.
A Cape with a rear lean-to; the front eave stays low.

constraints.statement: Eave height 8 ft 0 in to 9 ft 6 in above finished first floor, and the head of the first-floor window not more than 14 in below the underside of the cornice. This single rule separates every real Cape from every revival Cape.

test.note: Tests the window-head-to-cornice clause. Eave height (8ft-9ft6in) is the statement's other numeric claim and stays prose.

constraints.statement: No dormers on the front (street) roof slope. Rear-slope dormers are a permissible later addition; front dormers are not part of the type.
Roof pitch 9:12 to 12:12. Below 8:12 the loft is unusable and the house reads as minimal-traditional; above 12:12 it reads as a First Period two-storey house cut down.
Rake and eave trim not more than 6 in wide, returning 6–12 in at the corner. Full modillion cornices and deep returns belong to Georgian work.

test.note: The corner-return dimension (6-12in) is the statement's other numeric claim and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Roof and wall overhangs kept under 8 in on exposed coastal sites; shingle exposure 5–6 in; sill within 18 in of grade.

test.note: Tests the overhang clause. Shingle exposure and sill height are the statement's other numeric claims and stay prose.

exemplars.name: Atwood-Higgins House
exemplars.note: Built c. 1730 as a half house and expanded to a full Cape in the late 18th or early 19th century — the growth grammar preserved in one building. Now within Cape Cod National Seashore.
exemplars.why: Ernest Allen Connally's 1959 HABS survey of Cape Cod houses 'reported that this was locally considered to be the best example on Cape Cod' (HABS MA-1087), and it is the house the node's own growth grammar is written on -- a half house doubled to a full Cape.

exemplars.name: Jabez Wilder House
exemplars.note: Documented by HABS; a bow-roof ('rainbow roof') Cape, the coastal variant in which the rafters are given a slight convex curve. Date is traditional and not independently confirmed.
exemplars.why: The bow-roof ('rainbow roof') Cape the node's own note describes, drawn by HABS as MA-137 -- the coastal variant with the rafters given a slight convex curve, on the South Shore rather than the peninsula.

exemplars.name: Dillingham House
exemplars.note: Among the earliest Cape-form dwellings on the peninsula; substantially enlarged in the 18th century, so the original half-house core must be read through later fabric.
exemplars.why: Among the earliest Cape-form dwellings on the peninsula (the node's own note), a founding family's house in the town that is the type's hearth -- and, on Wikipedia's account, moved and raised to two storeys since, so regional rather than canonical.

exemplars.name: Elisha Cobb House
exemplars.note: A plain Outer Cape 'double house' of about 1800, grown from a house-and-a-half by the usual quarter, with the unusual twist of two short saltbox lean-tos behind instead of one: plank walls under shingle, one central brick stack, 9/6 sash, a box cornice, and hewn rafters about 4 by 10 on purlins. Inside the National Seashore and recorded by HABS with measured drawings, which is what it is here for.
exemplars.why: HABS MA-705 calls it 'a typical Cape Cod "double house"' and states its over-all dimensions, plank walls, single central stack, 9/6 sash and rafter size -- a plain measured specimen rather than a famous one, inside Cape Cod National Seashore.

exemplars.name: Swift-Daley House
exemplars.note: A full Cape of 1741 on the Outer Cape, built by Joshua Knowles with the bowed roof that Eastham's ship's carpenters gave their houses: wide board floors, a deep keeping-room fireplace and the narrow winder stair beside it. The house of Nathaniel Swift before he left for Chicago and the meat-packing trade; restored by the Daleys from 1939 and a museum of the Eastham Historical Society since 1974.
exemplars.why: The Outer Cape's variant stated by its keeper: the Eastham Historical Society dates it to 1741 by Joshua Knowles and calls its bowed roof 'typical of early houses built by ship's carpenters', the coastal form the node's note gives the Jabez Wilder House on the mainland.

sources: Abbott Lowell Cummings, The Framed Houses of Massachusetts Bay, 1625–1725 (1979)
J. Frederick Kelly, Early Domestic Architecture of Connecticut (1924)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
Dell Upton and John Michael Vlach, eds., Common Places: Readings in American Vernacular Architecture (1986)
Ernest Allen Connally, 'The Cape Cod House: An Introductory Study', Journal of the Society of Architectural Historians 19 (1960)

proportion_packs.note: The bay still generates the plan -- two rooms flanking the stack, the winder beside it -- but the storey is cut to one-and-a-half rather than two, which is a roof decision (see the massing entry), not a bay decision. The quarter/half/three-quarter/full growth grammar this node leads with is literally this pack's own resolution philosophy for material scarcity in practice: 'hold the bay at 16-20 ft and add bays rather than stretching one, which is what every historic plan type is a record of' (timber-bay's own material-availability conflict entry) -- a Cape is that principle built as a household's actual construction history, one bay added at a time as money allowed. No facade-system pack is bound: the door is deliberately off-centre until the growth sequence completes, which is the opposite of a composed front.

Roof pitch (9:12-12:12) follows the habitable-loft-versus-wind-load logic this node states directly, and it is a lower, steadier pitch than the two-storey types because the rafter is shorter over a smaller frame. The eave is this pack's near-zero default (6 in or less) -- and uniquely among the four New England nodes bound in this pass, the Cape KEEPS that flush eave through its whole 1700-1850 run rather than acquiring an 18th-century boxed cornice, which is exactly why 'window heads almost touching the cornice' survives as this node's single most reliable diagnostic tell (its own words) long after garrison and saltbox houses had picked up Georgian trim.

Governs the light-count date sequence across this node's unusually long 1700-1850 floruit, and its window_head_masonry rule (head at ~0.78-0.82 of storey) is the arithmetic behind this node's own hard constraint (c01): window head within 14 in of the cornice on an 8-9.5 ft eave.
Bound for the single head-datum rule only, as on the other three nodes in this family; the treatise's 13:6 window ratio is not this tradition's governing figure.

The hall-single-cell (half Cape) and hall-and-parlor (full Cape) room logic is identical to new-england-colonial's, and the pack's own room_adjacency_overrides note -- 'the whole Anglo-American folk-house catalogue is this arithmetic' -- is a direct statement of the growth grammar this node is organized around.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's own notes say what it dimensions: 'the 8-20 in cantilever of the second-floor girt past the wall below', and that 'THE MODULE IS THE JOIST, NOT THE BAY' because a jetty is a cantilever dimensioned by the member cantilevering. The Cape's record deletes that member by name -- no second storey, so no second plate and no second floor frame -- and there is no girt to cantilever and no post to cut a drop from. Both of the pack's two devices sit at a second-floor level this house does not have: the framed jetty with its bressumer and drops, and the hewn overhang chamfered out of a continuous post. This is the mechanism being absent rather than merely unused, which is the narrow case a decline is for.
declined_packs.quote: There is no second storey, so there is no second plate, no second floor frame
declined_packs.note: governs 0 slots on this node; --impact reports 'Declining it changes no dimension on this node.' No slot loses dimensioning.

declined_packs.reason: The pack says in its own module note what it is about, and it is not a category the Cape belongs to: 'the module cannot be a course of the wall. It is a course of the DRESSING -- the quoin, the jamb, the lintel, the mullion, the kneeler, the coping', on a rubble field wall that 'CANNOT MAKE A CORNER' and must therefore be quoined in dressed stone. This node states its wall in one clause and it is timber-framed and wood-clad -- clapboard, or white-cedar shingle at 5-6 in exposure -- so there is no rubble field to course, no dressed jamb to rebate a reveal into, and no quoin run to alternate. The contradiction is not the blanket kind the trap warns about: it is the node naming the wall material that the pack's entire module is derived from. Two of the delivered rules are visibly wrong on this house rather than merely inapplicable -- the graded stone-slate diminishing course reaching roof_material against a record that says the roof is of wood shingle, and 13 1/2 in of exposed stone plinth reaching foundation_expression against a record that says 'no raised basement, no water table of consequence'.
declined_packs.quote: Wall of clapboard or, on the outer Cape, unpainted white-cedar shingle
declined_packs.note: governs 10 slots; 2 lose all dimensioning -- foundation_expression and roof_material go to NOTHING. The other eight re-attribute: daylight_strategy, depth_and_pile, height_proportion, reveal_masonry and wing_strategy pass to timber-bay (bound by this node itself); window_head_masonry and window_proportion to sash-light (bound by this node itself); wall_thickness_masonry to facade-medieval-english from english-medieval-timber-frame. Losing the roof and foundation figures is the honest outcome here: what they carry today is a stone slate roof and a stone plinth on a wood-shingled house that declares neither.
